newsitem.title: UK: British economic boom will not save Major-analysts.
newsitem.headline: British economic boom will not save Major-analysts.

text.p: The current British government under John Major looks likely to be the first since the second World War to win an election during a recession and then lose one in the midst of an economic boom.
Britain is enjoying the kind of sustained growth governments have dreamed of achieving for decades -- but even economic nirvana looks unlikely to seal election victory.

Just months ahead of a general election, due by May 22, Prime Minister John Major is hoping the best economic conditions since the 1960s -- inflation at 2.5 percent, growth rising above 3.0 percent and unemployment tumbling -- will lure back voters.

Conservative strategists point to the April 1992 election, which they won even though the economy was sick with unemployment climbing and economic output weak. Now, the lively economic background could hardly be more fortuitous.

But, voting experts say, the economy is unlikely to tempt back enough voters and the opposition Labour party, around 20 percent ahead in polls, may simply end up inheriting a model economic upturn which could last a full parliamentary term.

"The strong economy will help narrow the large poll gap between the parties by election day but not enough to allow the Conservatives to win," said Neil Carter, voting specialist at the University of York.
Normally rising consumer confidence and economic success would boost government ratings, but the historic relationship between the two appears to have snapped.

The problem, analysts say, is the Conservatives have found it tough restoring their reputation for economic competence following the forced ejection of the pound out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) back in September 1992, while Labour's reputation, has been improving while in opposition.

The dilemma was highlighted by a MORI poll in mid-December that found 31 percent of respondents think Labour has the best economic policies, ahead of 28 percent for the Conservatives, even though Labour has been out of power since 1979.

"The economic upturn since 1992 has been largely due to our forced ejection for the ERM which the government tried to resist," said Jeremy Hawkins, analyst at Bank America. "The electorate has therefore been wary of crediting the government with the recovery."

So while the economy is booming, voters are reluctant to thank the Conservatives for the upturn and have warmed to Labour as its leadership moved away from the traditional tax-and-spend economic policies still favoured by many of its party activists.

A poll on January 5 for the Sunday Telegraph found two thirds of voters believe taxes will go up after the next election whichever party wins power. In the past, Labour has suffered because it alone was considered the high-tax party.

The government is hoping, of course, that the much-heralded return of the "feel-good" factor -- consumers feeling more confident and spending more -- will eventually feed through to the polls in coming months.

But analysts argue that consumers have actually felt better -- at least according to polls of confidence -- for at least the last two years, and this has not been accompanied by any decisive upturn in Conservative support.

A Gallup poll at the end of 1996 showed voters remarkably optimistic, with 37 percent of people believing 1997 would be better than 1996 compared with just 21 percent who said it would be worse -- one of the strongest optimism readings this decade. But still Conservative support is stuck at low levels.

"It takes a very long time for perceptions of an economic upturn to become established with the electorate...perceptions lag long behing economic reality," said Marian Bell, economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland.

Ironically, while the strong economy will undoubtedly tempt a large portion of voters back to the Conservatives, it may also have the perverse effect of making other voters more willing to take a risk with Labour, on the grounds the economy will continue to prosper whichever party is in power, analysts say.

In the April 1992 election, for example, many voters appeared wary of voting Labour (then associated with severe economic mismanagement in the 1970s) precisely because the economy was mired in recession and the spectre of higher taxes and mortgage rates (associated with Labour) was uppermost in peoples' minds.

James Alt, in his book The Politics of Economic Decline, has argued that affluence was necessary for voters to feel economically secure enough to support leftist policies of social reform and higher social spending.
But voting experts reckon Labour still has to be wary as any undermining of its reputation on economic issues -- such as any tax rises it might yet propose -- could do severe damage.
The party has failed to score 40 percent of the vote in the past six elections, and still needs a large swing of around 4.5 percent in the coming election to capture power.
